Peel a banana or a satsuma all by yourself.
Crack an egg into a bowl.
steps.note: Tap it on the edge once, thumbs in the crack, pull it apart over the bowl. Bits of shell can be fished out. Everybody's first one has shell in it.

steps.test: Make a sandwich and give it to somebody to eat.
steps.twist: Every part of it with the other hand.

categories.name: Money and business
categories.line: Handling it, earning it, selling, running something, investing.

tracks.name: Handling money
tracks.line: Naming coins to a weekly shop.

steps.test: Name every coin and note when somebody holds one up.
how: Get somebody to lay out all the coins and notes.
Name each one, then shut your eyes and name three by feel.
The two-pound and the ten-pence catch everybody out.

steps.test: Count out one pound in three different ways.
Pay for something yourself and check the change is right.
Give correct change from a five-pound note, five times running.
steps.note: Five times running with no mistakes. Count it back into their hand out loud.

steps.test: Keep a written record of money in and out for a month, and balance it.
Do a full weekly shop to a budget and come in under it.

tracks.name: Earning
tracks.line: One job to paying somebody else.

steps.test: Do one real job and be paid for it.
Do a job for somebody outside your own family.
Hold a paid job around the place for a season, and turn up for it.
Save half of everything you earn for a month.
Turn ten pounds into thirty pounds honestly, and show your working.
steps.note: Honestly means you made something or did something, not that somebody gave it to you.

steps.test: Pay another person a fair share for their part in something you ran.

tracks.name: Selling
tracks.line: One thing to one person, to a real product.

steps.test: Sell one thing to one person.
Run a stall with real money and real change.
Sell to ten people you have never met.
Price something so it sells, and defend the price when asked.
steps.note: Defending the price means saying what it cost you and why it is worth it, without apologising.

steps.test: Handle somebody being unhappy with what you sold, and put it right.
Make something strangers buy more than once.

tracks.name: Running something
tracks.line: A plan on paper to being asked back.

steps.test: Write down on paper what a small event would need.
Run one part of an outing yourself.
Organise a small event for the group and make it happen.
Make an event cover its own costs with nobody topping it up.
steps.note: Covering its costs means the money in is at least the money out. Write both down before you start.

steps.test: Find out what people actually want first, then do that.
Run something people ask you to do again.

tracks.name: Making money grow
tracks.line: Saving to understanding it.

steps.test: Save for four weeks without spending any of it.
Explain what interest is, in your own words, correctly.
steps.note: Interest is money paid for the use of money. Try explaining it with a real example, not a definition.

steps.test: Buy something, improve it, and sell it for more.
Explain what a share in a company actually is.
Track a small investment for six months and explain what happened.
Teach a younger child what saving and interest mean.

tracks.name: Negotiating
tracks.line: Asking to a fair deal.

steps.test: Ask for something you want, out loud, in a full sentence.
Swap something with somebody so you are both pleased.
Ask for a better price and get one.
steps.note: Ask politely and be willing to hear no. Markets, car boot sales and second-hand things are the places to try.

steps.test: Walk away from a deal that was not good enough.
Sort out a disagreement where both sides end up content.
Negotiate something real on behalf of somebody else.

categories.name: Beauty and buildings
categories.line: Why one street feels good and another does not. Shapes, proportion, arches, and your own town.

tracks.name: Looking at buildings
tracks.line: Noticing, then being able to say why.

steps.test: Point at a building you think is pretty and one you think is ugly, and say which is which.
how: Stand somewhere you can see several buildings at once.
Point at the one you would most like to look at every day.
Then point at the one you would least like to look at.
Say which is which out loud. That is the whole level — you do not have to justify it yet.

steps.test: Say one reason why. Any reason counts, including a feeling.
steps.note: A feeling is a real reason. 'It looks friendly' or 'the windows are all different sizes' both count.

steps.test: Find two buildings on the same street and say which you would rather live in, and why.
Photograph three you like and three you do not, then find one thing the good ones share.
steps.note: Look for the things they share rather than the things you like. Often it is even windows, a proper roof, or that the door is where you expect.

steps.test: Walk somebody round and show them the good and the bad, and have them see it too.
Write down, in your own words, five rules for what makes a building good.

tracks.name: Proportion
tracks.line: Why some shapes feel right and others do not.

steps.test: Fold a piece of string exactly in half by eye, then check it.
how: Cut a piece of string about as long as your arm.
Fold it where you THINK the middle is. Do not measure first.
Now bring the two ends together and see how close you were.
Do it three times. You get better at it very quickly, and that is the point.

steps.test: Look at two rectangles and say which one feels nicer to you. There is no wrong answer.
steps.note: There genuinely is no wrong answer. Most people pick a rectangle roughly half again as long as it is wide, and nobody knows why.

steps.test: Draw a house and put the door at a size that looks right for a person.
steps.note: A door is about twice as tall as it is wide, and a person is about three doors tall on a normal house.

steps.test: Divide a line into three equal parts by eye, then measure and see how close you got.
Find something around you about one and a half times as long as it is wide, and prove it with a ruler.
steps.note: About one and a half to one. A bank card, a book, a window — measure the long side and the short side and divide.

steps.test: Draw the front of a building where every part looks right beside every other part.

tracks.name: Shapes and geometry
tracks.line: Circles, squares, tiles and solids.

steps.test: Find a circle, a square and a triangle in the room you are in.
how: Look around the room you are in right now.
A circle: a plate, a clock, a door handle. A square: a tile, a window, a book.
A triangle is the hard one — try a roof, a coat hanger, a slice of something.
Point at each and name it.

steps.test: Draw a circle freehand that somebody else agrees is properly round.
Draw a square and check its corners against the corner of a page.
Make a shape that tiles, and fit six of them together with no gaps.
steps.note: Squares, triangles and hexagons tile on their own. Circles never do, which is why floors are not made of them.

steps.test: Step a compass around a circle six times and have it close exactly on itself.
steps.note: Keep the compass exactly the same width the whole way round. If it closes on itself, you have drawn a hexagon.

steps.test: Cut and fold paper into a solid shape — a cube, or a pyramid that stands up.

tracks.name: Symmetry and pattern
tracks.line: Repeats, mirrors, and why they calm a room.

steps.test: Fold paper, cut a shape, open it out, and see the two halves match.
how: Fold a sheet of paper in half and press the crease flat.
Cut a shape out of the FOLDED edge — do not cut the fold away completely.
Open it out. Whatever you cut on one side has appeared on the other.
That is symmetry, and you just made some.

steps.test: Find three symmetrical things around you.
Make a pattern that repeats six times without a mistake.
Draw the missing half of a face or a building so both sides match.
Find a symmetrical building and a lopsided one, and say which feels calmer to stand in front of.
steps.note: Most old public buildings are symmetrical and most modern ones are not. Notice which one your eye settles on.

steps.test: Design a tile that still works when you repeat it in every direction.

tracks.name: Arches and columns
tracks.line: The old ways, and why they were used.

steps.test: Find an arch somewhere near you and stand underneath it.
how: Arches are over doorways, under bridges, in old churches and railway stations.
Find one and go and stand underneath it.
Look up. Notice the stones or bricks are wedge shaped and lean on each other.

steps.test: Build an arch out of blocks that stands up on its own.
steps.note: Build the two sides up leaning inwards, and the last stone at the very top is the one that locks it. Bricks or wooden blocks both work.

steps.test: Point out the three parts of a column — the base, the shaft and the top.
steps.note: The base is what it stands on, the shaft is the tall part, the top is called the capital.

steps.test: Say in your own words why an arch holds more weight than a flat beam.
steps.note: An arch pushes the weight sideways into the walls instead of hanging it in the middle, which is where a flat beam breaks.

steps.test: Find a column, an arch and a dome all in one day.
Explain to somebody younger why old buildings were built this way.

tracks.name: Your own town
tracks.line: Reading the place you actually live.

steps.test: Walk down your street and count the buildings you like.
how: Walk the length of one street, slowly, looking up rather than ahead.
Count the buildings you actually like the look of.
Say the number out loud at the end. Most people are surprised how low it is.

steps.test: Find the oldest building near you and say what is different about it.
steps.note: Older usually means smaller windows, thicker walls, more stone, and more bother taken over the bits near the door.

steps.test: Draw a map of one street with the good buildings marked on it.
Find a spot in your town that feels good to stand in, and say what makes it so.
steps.note: Places that feel good are often enclosed but not closed in — something to look at, somewhere to sit, and not too much noise.

steps.test: Find a spot that feels bad to stand in, and say what would fix it.
Take somebody round and show them the town the way you now see it.

categories.name: The classical mind
categories.line: Logic, the big questions, the great stories, and one beautiful thing a day.

tracks.name: Spotting a bad argument
tracks.line: Telling a good argument from a loud one.

steps.test: Notice somebody changing the subject instead of answering, and say so afterwards.
how: Listen for it in a real conversation, not in a book.
Somebody asks a question, and the answer is about something else entirely.
Do not interrupt. Afterwards, say to somebody what actually happened.
Once you have heard it once you will hear it constantly.

steps.test: Say what is wrong with 'everybody does it, so it must be fine'.
steps.note: Lots of people doing a thing does not make it right, and never did. That is all you need to say.

steps.test: Spot three different bad arguments in a week and write down what was wrong with each.
Name five kinds of bad argument and give a real example of each.
steps.note: Attacking the person instead of the point, either-or when there are more options, everybody-does-it, one story treated as proof, and slippery slopes.

steps.test: Point one out kindly, in the moment, without making anybody feel small.
Teach somebody younger how to tell a good argument from a loud one.

tracks.name: Asking the good question
tracks.line: The Socratic habit, at any age.

steps.test: Ask why three times in a row about the same thing and see where you end up.
how: Pick anything. Why is the sky blue, why do we go to bed, why is that rule there.
Whatever answer you get, ask why again.
Then once more. Three deep is usually where it gets interesting.
Ask kindly, not to catch anybody out.

steps.test: Ask somebody what a word really means, and keep going until it is clear.
Take a word like fair or brave and give an example and a non-example.
Ask questions for five whole minutes without giving your own opinion once.
Change your own mind out loud, because of an answer somebody gave you.
Run a question with a group and keep everybody talking.

tracks.name: The big questions
tracks.line: Philosophy, done out loud, from about five upwards.

steps.test: Say what you think the word good means, in your own words.
how: Not the dictionary meaning — what YOU think it means.
Try finishing this: something is good when...
Give an example of something good and something not good, and see if your rule fits both.
There is no right answer here and that is the point.

steps.test: Answer this and give a reason: is it ever right to tell a lie?
If every plank of a ship is replaced one by one, is it still the same ship? Say why.
steps.note: It is called the Ship of Theseus and adults have argued about it for two thousand years. There is no answer, only better reasons.

steps.test: Argue properly for the opposite of what you actually believe.
Read a page of a philosopher and say one thing you agreed with and one you did not.
Run a proper discussion for the group and let the best answer win, even if it is not yours.

tracks.name: The great stories
tracks.line: Myths, fables, and the books people keep reading.

steps.test: Listen to a whole myth or fable and say what happened.
Say what the story was actually about, underneath the events.
Tell one from memory to somebody else.
Read a whole book that people have been reading for hundreds of years.
steps.note: Homer, the Odyssey, Aesop, the Norse or Irish myths, Robinson Crusoe, Treasure Island. Old enough that your grandparents' grandparents read it.

steps.test: Find the same idea turning up in two different old stories.
Read one aloud to the younger ones, doing the voices.

tracks.name: Words and where they come from
tracks.line: Latin and Greek, the useful way.

steps.test: Learn what one word root means and find two English words that use it.
how: Try 'aqua', which means water. Aquarium. Aqueduct.
Or 'photo', which means light. Photograph. Photosynthesis.
Pick one, learn what it means, and find two English words built on it.

steps.test: Learn ten roots and what they mean.
Work out a long word you have never seen before, from its parts alone.
steps.note: Break it into pieces first. Tele means far, scope means to look. Bio means life, logy means the study of.

steps.test: Learn twenty Latin or Greek words and use them correctly.
Read one line of Latin or Greek and say what it means.
Teach somebody to break a long word into its parts.

tracks.name: One beautiful thing a day
tracks.line: Looking on purpose, and keeping what is worth keeping.

steps.test: Find one beautiful thing today and say why it is.
how: It can be anything — a tree, a chair, a bit of sky, a face, a sound.
Stop and look at it properly for ten seconds rather than glancing.
Then say out loud what makes it beautiful. Trying to say it is most of the exercise.

steps.test: Do it every day for a week.
Do it every day for a month and write each one down.
Keep a commonplace book for a month — copy in anything worth keeping.
steps.note: A commonplace book is just a notebook where you copy anything worth keeping — a line, a fact, a bit of a poem. People have kept them for centuries.

steps.test: Learn one piece of music, one poem or one painting well enough to describe it from memory.
Show somebody something beautiful they had been walking past for years.

tracks.name: Thinking on your own
tracks.line: A walk, a question, and no screen.

steps.test: Walk or sit for ten minutes with nothing to look at, thinking about one thing.
how: No phone, no book, no music, nobody talking to you.
Walk, or sit somewhere you can see out.
Pick one question before you start and stay with it for ten minutes.
Boredom for the first two minutes is normal. Go past it.
steps.note: This is genuinely hard the first time and gets easy fast. Ten minutes without input is where most of your own ideas live.

steps.test: Say afterwards what you worked out.
Write down what you actually think about something, a page of it.
Do that every week for a month.
Change your mind on paper, and write down what changed it.
Keep it going for a whole season.

categories.name: Nerve
categories.line: Small brave things, done on purpose, until they stop being brave. The later levels are for older ones and adults.

tracks.name: Asking out loud
tracks.line: From the time of day to the thing you actually want.

steps.test: Ask a stranger the time, or for directions you do not really need.
how: Pick somebody who does not look busy.
Make eye contact first, then ask. Excuse me, do you have the time?
Say thank you and walk on. That is the whole thing.
It takes about eight seconds and it is the doorway to all the rest.

steps.test: Ask for something small in a shop — a bag, a glass of water, what they would recommend.
Ask politely for a discount, and take no cheerfully.
steps.note: Ask once, pleasantly, and mean it. If it is no, say thanks anyway and be genuinely fine about it — that part is the skill.

steps.test: Ask somebody for a favour you would normally talk yourself out of asking for.
Ask for something you genuinely want, from somebody who could actually say yes.
Take somebody else out and get them to do their first ask.

tracks.name: Walking in
tracks.line: Rooms where you know nobody.

steps.test: Walk into a room where you know nobody, and stay.
how: A class, a club, a talk, a group at a day out — anywhere you know nobody.
Go in and stay at least twenty minutes. Leaving early is the thing to beat.
You do not have to talk to anybody the first time. Staying is the level.

steps.test: Join a class or a group where everybody already knows each other.
Sit down with people you have never met and start a conversation.
steps.note: Ask whatever you actually want to know. Looking at things is what a shop is for, and staff are there to be asked.

steps.test: Turn up to something on your own, having told nobody you were coming.
steps.note: You are not obliged to buy anything and you do not owe anybody an explanation. You are deciding whether you like it, which is exactly what a customer does. Behave like one, ask your questions, and leave when you have your answer.

steps.test: Go to something where you are the only one of your kind in the room.
Bring somebody who would never have gone on their own.

tracks.name: On the phone
tracks.line: The call you would rather send a message about.

steps.test: Make one phone call you would rather have sent a message about.
how: Pick the one that has been sitting on your list.
Write down the one sentence you need to say, then dial before you reread it.
It is nearly always shorter and easier than the version in your head.

steps.test: Phone a shop and ask whether they have something.
Phone somewhere expensive and ask real questions about what they do.
steps.note: Ask what you want to know the way any caller would. You do not have to hand over your life story or your details to find out what something costs.

steps.test: Phone to sort out something that went wrong, politely, and get it put right.
Phone a stranger to ask for information, advice or an introduction.
Make five calls in one day that you had been putting off.

tracks.name: Getting told no
tracks.line: Collecting refusals until they stop stinging.

steps.test: Ask for something you are fairly sure will be refused, and be refused.
how: Ask for something small and unreasonable but harmless — a free coffee, a look behind the counter.
Be pleasant. You are not trying to trick anybody.
When they say no, smile, say no problem, and go. The no is the point, not the thing.
steps.note: This is sometimes called rejection practice. The aim is to find out that a no costs you nothing at all.

steps.test: Collect three noes in a week, on purpose.
Collect ten noes, and notice that nothing bad happened.
Ask one more question after a no, instead of walking off.
Turn a no into a yes by asking a different way.
steps.note: Usually it is asking for something smaller, asking a different person, or simply explaining why you are asking.

steps.test: Take somebody else out collecting noes.

tracks.name: Speaking up on the spot
tracks.line: No warning, no notes.

steps.test: Say something out loud in a group of people you do not know.
how: A queue, a class, a waiting room, a group at a day out.
One sentence out loud that other people can hear. A question is easiest.
Your heart will go faster than the situation deserves. That is the muscle working.

steps.test: Ask a question at a talk or an event, in front of everybody.
Stand up and thank somebody publicly, in a room.
Speak for two minutes with no warning at all.
Speak up when something is wrong and nobody else has.
Take a microphone you were not expecting to be handed.

tracks.name: Not minding what people think
tracks.line: Harmless, cheerful, and entirely your own business.

steps.test: Wear something you would normally think twice about, for a whole day.
how: A bright coat, an odd hat, colours you would not usually put together.
Wear it all day, including where people know you.
Count how many people actually say anything. It is almost always nobody.

steps.test: Hum or sing out loud somewhere people can hear you.
Dance where people can see you.
Sit alone in a café for an hour with no phone out.
steps.note: An hour is longer than it sounds. Bring nothing. Watch the room, think, or do nothing at all.

steps.test: Do something harmlessly odd in public and stay for the reaction.
steps.note: Harmless is the whole rule. Nobody inconvenienced, nobody frightened, nothing damaged, and stop the moment it stops being cheerful.

steps.test: Do the thing you have been putting off purely because of what people would think.

categories.name: Negotiation
categories.line: Almost everything is flexible — the price, the terms, the timing. Most people simply never ask.

tracks.name: Asking for a better price
tracks.line: From asking at home to shifting a printed price tag.

steps.test: Ask somebody at home for something you want, and give one good reason why they should say yes.
how: Pick something you actually want — later bedtime, a lift somewhere, a thing you would like.
Ask plainly, then give ONE reason why it is a good idea for them, not just for you.
Then stop talking and let them answer. The silence is the hard part.
That is a negotiation. You have just done one.

steps.test: Find out what somebody else pays for something you pay for — a phone, a haircut, a subscription.
Ask for a discount in a shop or at a market, out loud, once.
steps.note: Say it plainly and pleasantly: is there any movement on the price? Then stop talking. Markets, independent shops and anything second-hand are the easiest places to start.

steps.test: Get three different prices for the same thing before you buy anything.
Get money off by asking, then write down the exact words that worked.
Get a better price on something that had a printed price tag on it.
steps.note: A printed price feels fixed and mostly is not — especially on the last one, a display model, something marked, or when you are buying more than one.

tracks.name: Asking for more instead of less
tracks.line: Value is easier to move than price.

steps.test: Ask for something extra that costs them nothing — a bag, more sauce, a longer look.
how: Anywhere that serves you — a café, a shop, a takeaway.
Ask for something small that costs them nothing at all.
Ask pleasantly and as if it is completely normal, because it is.
Notice how often the answer is simply yes.

steps.test: Ask for a free upgrade somewhere, pleasantly, and take no cheerfully.
Get something added in for nothing — delivery, a case, an extra portion, a longer guarantee.
When the price will not move, ask what else they can do instead.
steps.note: This is the most useful question in the whole category. If the price is fixed, the extras usually are not.

steps.test: Get an upgrade on something that actually mattered — a seat, a room, a service.
Show somebody else that asking for more is easier than asking for less.

tracks.name: From your chair
tracks.line: The bills you have never once questioned.

steps.test: Find one thing your household pays every month and work out what it costs in a year.
how: Phone, streaming, insurance, broadband, a gym, a subscription.
Find the monthly amount and multiply it by twelve.
Write that yearly number down and look at it. Most people have never seen it.

steps.test: Look up what a brand new customer pays for that same thing.
Phone them and ask, plainly, whether that is the best they can do.
steps.note: Ask for what any customer would ask for. You do not owe them a reason and you do not have to threaten to leave.

steps.test: Ask to be put through to somebody who can actually change it.
steps.note: The first person you speak to often cannot change anything. Retentions, customer loyalty or a supervisor usually can.

steps.test: Get a rate, a fee or a bill reduced by asking for it.
Go through every regular bill you have in one afternoon.

tracks.name: Terms, not just the price
tracks.line: The price is often the least flexible part.

steps.test: Write down three things about something you are buying that are not the price.
how: Think of anything you are about to buy, big or small.
Write down three things that matter besides the price — when it arrives, how long it is guaranteed, whether you can send it back.
Those three are usually easier to move than the price is.

steps.test: Ask when it could arrive, and whether sooner is possible.
Ask for longer to pay, or to pay in parts.
Ask for a better guarantee or a longer window to change your mind.
Improve a deal without the price changing at all.
Explain to somebody why the price is usually the last thing to move.

tracks.name: Being willing to walk away
tracks.line: The quietest strength there is.

steps.test: Before you go, write down the number you will not go above.
how: Decide the number BEFORE you are standing in front of the thing.
Write it on your hand or on your phone.
A number decided in advance is worth ten decided on the spot.

steps.test: Leave something in a shop that you wanted, because it was not right.
steps.note: You have not lost anything. Wanting something is not the same as needing it today.

steps.test: Say out loud 'that is more than I want to spend', and then stop talking.
Walk away from a deal, and be glad about it afterwards.
Have somebody come back to you with a better offer after you left.
Walk away from something you really wanted, because the terms were wrong.

tracks.name: Both sides pleased
tracks.line: The deals people come back for.

steps.test: Swap something with somebody so that you are both happy.
Ask somebody what they actually need before you say what you want.
steps.note: People will tell you what they need if you ask. It is very often not the thing you assumed.

steps.test: Do a deal where the other person clearly got something they wanted too.
Settle a disagreement so both people came away with most of it.
Do a deal that somebody thanks you for afterwards.
Become somebody people want to deal with again.

categories.name: You belong here
categories.line: Fine shops, grand rooms and expensive things — so you never again decide somewhere is above you.

tracks.name: From where you are sitting
tracks.line: All of this can start today, at home.

steps.test: Look up a grand building near you that is open to the public, and find its opening times.
how: Try the city hall, the courthouse, a cathedral, a university, a museum, a big old library.
Search the name plus 'opening times' or 'visitors'.
Most of them are open to anybody and free, and almost nobody knows it.
You are not going today. You are just finding out that you could.

steps.test: Look up the real price of something you would never normally price — a watch, a car, a suite.
Phone a dealership and ask two questions about a model. Two minutes, then thank them and go.
steps.note: Ask two real questions — what engine, what it costs, when it is available. Two minutes, thank them, done. You are not committing to anything by asking.

steps.test: Phone a fine hotel and ask what is included in a room.
Contact somewhere you assume would never reply, and ask something real.
Book something in advance that you would normally have talked yourself out of.

tracks.name: Fine shops
tracks.line: Looking properly, and being helped.

steps.test: Walk into an expensive shop and look at three things properly, without hurrying.
how: Somewhere you would normally walk past because of the prices in the window.
Go in, and look at three things properly — pick them up if they can be picked up.
Nobody is going to ask you to leave. Looking is what the shop is for.
Leave when you are finished, not when you start feeling awkward.

steps.test: Let an assistant come over, and tell them what you are looking at.
Ask to try something on — a watch, a coat, a jacket.
steps.note: Trying something on is normal and expected, and it is what the mirror is there for. Nobody is keeping score.

steps.test: Try on something far beyond what you would ever spend, and look in the mirror.
Spend half an hour somewhere expensive without buying and without apologising.
Take somebody who would never have gone in on their own.

tracks.name: Cars
tracks.line: Sitting in it is free.

steps.test: Look up a car you like and read what it actually costs.
how: Pick a car you have always liked the look of.
Find the real price, and the monthly figure if it is leased.
Knowing the actual number takes most of the mystery out of it.

steps.test: Walk into a dealership and look at one car, unhurried.
Sit in it, adjust the seat, and stay there a few minutes.
steps.note: Ask if you may sit in it and they will nearly always say yes. Take your time. Adjust the seat. It is allowed.

steps.test: Ask the questions you actually want answered.
Take a test drive.
Take somebody else for their first look.

tracks.name: Grand rooms
tracks.line: Most of them are open, and most people never check.

steps.test: Find out which grand buildings near you are open to the public.
steps.note: City halls, courthouses, cathedrals, university buildings, old libraries and many galleries are open to anybody and free. Almost nobody realises.

steps.test: Walk into a fine hotel lobby and sit down for ten minutes.
Visit the city hall, the courthouse, a gallery or a cathedral, and look up.
Have a coffee or afternoon tea somewhere far smarter than you would normally.
Go to an event in a building you had assumed was not for you.
Eat alone in a good restaurant, with no phone on the table.
steps.note: No phone, no book. Just you, the food, and the room. It is far easier than people expect and it changes something.

tracks.name: Carrying yourself
tracks.line: Not shrinking is a physical habit.

steps.test: Walk into a room with your head up and make eye contact with one person.
how: Head up, shoulders back, and slow down rather than speed up.
Find one person and meet their eyes for about a second.
That is it. It is a physical habit and it rewires surprisingly fast.

steps.test: Take up your full space — do not shrink, and do not hurry through.
Let somebody serve you without apologising for the trouble.
steps.note: Sorry-for-the-trouble is a habit, not manners. Thank you does the same job without shrinking.

steps.test: Take a compliment with a thank you, and nothing after it.
Ask for what you want in a room where you feel out of place.
Notice that you have stopped feeling out of place, and say when it changed.

tracks.name: The story you tell yourself
tracks.line: Testing the thing you assume would happen.

steps.test: Write down one place you avoid because you have decided it is not for you.
how: Be honest and be specific. Not 'posh places' but the actual shop, street or building.
One is enough to start with.
Keep the paper. You are going to check it against what actually happens.

steps.test: Write down what you assume would happen there. Keep the paper.
Notice one time you talked yourself out of something, and write down the exact thought.
Go to the place, and compare what happened with what you wrote.
steps.note: Read what you wrote before you went, then write what actually happened. The gap between the two is the whole point of this track.

steps.test: Go somewhere every week for a month that you used to avoid.
Tell somebody the story you used to believe, and what actually happened instead.

categories.name: Home and repair
categories.line: Keeping a place, mending, tools, bikes, first aid, engines.

tracks.name: Keeping a place
tracks.line: Your own things to the whole house.

steps.test: Put your own things away without being asked twice.
how: Look round the room for the things that are yours.
Put each one back where it actually lives, not on a pile.
Do it without anybody asking you twice.

steps.test: Sweep a floor and get the whole pile into the bin.
Wash up a full sink and put everything back where it lives.
Clean a room properly enough that it passes a close look.
steps.note: A close look means somebody else checks the corners, the skirting and behind the door.

steps.test: Do a load of washing from the basket to folded and put away.
Look after the house for a whole day — food, tidy, animals, all of it.

tracks.name: Mending
tracks.line: A screw to fixing things for other people.

steps.test: Tighten a loose screw with the right screwdriver.
how: Find a screw that is loose — a door handle, a chair, a hinge.
Match the screwdriver to the screw head. The wrong one chews it up.
Push in hard while you turn. Most of the work is pushing, not turning.
Turn clockwise until it is snug, then stop.

steps.test: Glue something so it stays fixed a month later.
Sew or patch something back into use.
steps.note: Take the tube out, find the hole in water, patch it, and it should hold overnight.

steps.test: Fix something rather than replacing it, three times.
Put up a shelf that is level and holds weight.
Fix something for somebody else who could not.

tracks.name: Tools
tracks.line: Naming them to teaching safety.

steps.test: Name ten tools and say what each one is for.
how: Open the toolbox and take ten things out.
Name each and say what it does. Guessing is allowed.
Put them all back where they came from.

steps.test: Use a hammer, a saw and a screwdriver safely.
Use a drill safely and put it away properly.
Put every tool back clean and where it lives, all season.
steps.note: Where it lives means the same place every time, so the next person can find it.

steps.test: Choose the right tool for a job without asking anybody.
Teach tool safety to younger children.

tracks.name: Bike mechanics
tracks.line: Pumping a tyre to a full service.

steps.test: Pump a tyre to the right pressure.
Put a chain back on and clean your hands afterwards.
Mend a puncture so it holds.
Adjust brakes so they bite properly.
steps.note: The brakes should bite before the lever reaches the handlebar, and the wheel should still spin freely.

steps.test: Take a wheel off and put it back on true.
Service somebody else's bike so they can ride it safely.

tracks.name: First aid
tracks.line: Calling for help to being the one they turn to.

steps.test: Know how to call for help and exactly what to say.
how: 999 in the UK and Ireland, and ask for ambulance, fire or police.
Say where you are first — the address before anything else.
Then what happened, how many people, and stay on the line.

steps.test: Clean and cover a cut properly.
Treat a burn, a sting and a nosebleed correctly.
Put somebody in the recovery position.
steps.note: The recovery position keeps somebody breathing if they are unconscious. Learn it from a real course or a first aid site.

steps.test: Pass a real first aid course.
Be the person the group turns to when somebody is hurt.

tracks.name: How things work
tracks.line: Taking one apart to putting it back.

steps.test: Take something broken apart and name five parts inside.
Explain how one everyday machine works, correctly.
steps.note: A kettle, a bicycle gear, a toilet cistern or a door lock. Say it in order — what happens first, then what.

steps.test: Take something apart and put it back so it still works.
Find out why something stopped working and say why.
Repair a small motor or appliance.
Explain it to somebody else so they could do it.

tracks.name: Staying safe
tracks.line: Your address to looking after others.

steps.test: Say your own address and a phone number from memory.
Know what to do if you get separated in a busy place.
Cross a road safely on your own, every time.
Know what to do in a fire and where everybody meets.
Judge a risk out loud before doing something, and change the plan.
steps.note: Say it out loud before you do it: what could go wrong, how likely, and what you will change.

steps.test: Be responsible for a younger child's safety for a whole day.

categories.name: Care and kindness
categories.line: Animals, younger ones, older people, giving, the community.

tracks.name: Animals
tracks.line: Feeding to raising.

steps.test: Feed an animal the right amount, every day, for a week.
how: Find out how much this animal should get. Guessing is how animals get ill.
Feed it at about the same time each day.
Fresh water every time as well, not just food.

steps.test: Do the unpleasant half of caring for one, not just the nice half.
Look after an animal completely, on your own, for a week.
Notice an animal is unwell before anybody says, and tell somebody.
steps.note: Off its food, hiding, breathing oddly, or just not behaving like itself. Say so early rather than waiting.

steps.test: Raise something from young.
Teach another child to care for an animal properly.

tracks.name: Younger ones
tracks.line: Including them to looking after a family.

steps.test: Notice a younger child on their own and bring them into the game.
Teach one younger child one thing you can do.
Look after a younger child for an hour and everybody is happy at the end.
steps.note: Happy at the end is the test, for both of you. An hour is enough to count.

steps.test: Get a younger child through their first hard walk, to the end, happy.
Run an activity for a group of younger children.
Look after a family who are new, through their whole first season.

tracks.name: Older people
tracks.line: Hello, to keeping it up.

steps.test: Say hello to somebody much older and shake their hand properly.
Visit somebody older and listen to them for an hour.
Do a job for a neighbour and take nothing for it.
Write down somebody's story from their own telling.
steps.note: Write it down as they said it, not tidied up. Ask when, where and who, and let them talk.

steps.test: Organise something for people who are on their own.
Keep it up for a year.

tracks.name: Giving
tracks.line: Sharing to a habit other people copy.

steps.test: Share something you actually wanted, before being asked.
Give away something you liked.
Raise money for something that is not for you.
steps.note: Not for you means you get nothing out of it, including the credit.

steps.test: Give a share of what you earned away on purpose.
Do something kind that nobody asked you to do.
Make giving a habit that somebody else starts copying.

tracks.name: Your own patch
tracks.line: One bit of litter to a whole shore.

steps.test: Pick up litter you walk past, without being asked.
Fill a bag from one beach or one path.
Look after one small public place for a month.
steps.note: One small place means the same place, more than once — a lane, a corner of a beach, a bus shelter.

steps.test: Get three other people to help you.
Organise a clean-up for the group.
Make it happen every season for a year.

tracks.name: Welcoming
tracks.line: Saying hello to running the welcome.

steps.test: Say hello first to somebody new, before they say it to you.
Show a new person where everything is.
Learn and use the names of five people you have just met.
Sit with somebody who came on their own.
Introduce two people to each other and get them talking.
steps.note: Introducing people properly means giving each of them something to say next.

steps.test: Run the welcome for a new family on their first day.

tracks.name: Helping
tracks.line: From four, beside you. One thing carried, one thing given, one thing done before anybody asked.

steps.test: Carry one thing to the table before a meal, and one thing back after it.
Put your own plate and cup by the sink when you have finished.
Give a pet its food, or a plant its water.
steps.note: No pet and no plant? Fill somebody's water glass before they ask for it.

steps.test: Make something for somebody and give it to them. A drawing counts.
Help a smaller child do something they cannot do yet, without doing it for them.
steps.note: Shoes, a zip, a puzzle piece. Hands off, words on.

steps.test: Do one helpful thing before anybody asks, and do not tell them it was you.

categories.name: Focus and calm
categories.line: Stillness, attention, sleep, fasting, gratitude, doing hard things.

tracks.name: Sitting still
tracks.line: One minute to twenty.

steps.test: Sit completely still and quiet for one minute.
how: Sit somewhere comfortable and set a timer for one minute.
Hands still, feet still, eyes open or shut, whichever.
Your mind will wander. That is fine and not a failure.
One minute is longer than you think, and that is the point.

steps.test: Sit still for five minutes without fidgeting.
steps.note: Fidgeting includes scratching and shifting about. Notice it, stop, carry on.

steps.test: Sit for ten minutes and notice your own breathing.
Sit for twenty minutes.
Do it every morning for thirty days.
Lead five minutes of stillness for the group.

tracks.name: Attention
tracks.line: One task to deep work.

steps.test: Do one thing for ten minutes with nothing else going on.
how: Pick one thing and put everything else out of reach.
Set a timer for ten minutes and start.
If you drift, come back. Drifting is not failing.

steps.test: Do one thing for twenty-five minutes without stopping.
steps.note: Twenty-five minutes is one pomodoro. Phone in another room, not face down beside you.

steps.test: Work for an hour with no screen near you.
Notice yourself drifting and come back, on purpose, five times.
Do a whole morning of one thing.
Explain to somebody else how you get yourself to concentrate.

tracks.name: Sleep
tracks.line: Going to bed to running your own rest.

steps.test: Go to bed without a fight, seven nights running.
Get up at the same time seven days running.
Notice how you feel after a bad night, and say so.
Keep screens out of the last hour before bed for two weeks.
steps.note: The last hour means no screens at all. Read, talk, or do something with your hands.

steps.test: Run your own bedtime with nobody reminding you, for a month.
Explain what sleep does, and help somebody else fix theirs.

tracks.name: Doing hard things
tracks.line: Not giving up to choosing the hard one.

steps.test: Finish something you wanted to give up on.
Keep going for ten minutes after it stopped being fun.
steps.note: Ten minutes past the point where you wanted to stop. Notice how it feels afterwards.

steps.test: Try something you are bad at, in front of other people.
Fail at something publicly and go back and do it again.
Choose the harder of two options on purpose, and say why.
Help somebody else through the moment they want to quit.

tracks.name: Noticing the good
tracks.line: One thing to a habit.

steps.test: Say one good thing about today, out loud, at tea.
Do it every day for a week.
Thank somebody properly, to their face, for something specific.
steps.note: Specific means what they actually did, not 'thanks for everything'.

steps.test: Write a thank-you letter that somebody keeps.
Do the daily one for thirty days.
Start it at a table where nobody was doing it.

tracks.name: Fasting
tracks.line: Twelve hours to thirty-six, without drama.
tracks.warn: Adults only past step five. Not if you are pregnant, diabetic, underweight, still growing, on medication that needs food, or have ever had trouble with eating. Children stop at step four — going without snacks is theirs; going without meals is not.

steps.test: Eat nothing between your meals for one whole day.
steps.note: Meals only. No picking, no snacks. Most people have never once done this.

steps.test: Do that on three separate days in one week.
Drink a glass of water when you think you are hungry, and wait ten minutes.
steps.note: Half the time it was thirst. You will be surprised how often.

steps.test: Finish eating by eight in the evening, three nights running.
Go twelve hours with nothing but water. Sleep counts for most of it.
steps.note: Eight in the evening to eight in the morning. Almost everybody has done this by accident.

steps.test: Do twelve hours on three separate days in one week.
Push your first meal to midday. Fourteen hours, water only.
steps.note: From here on this ladder is for adults. See the note at the top.

steps.test: Do fourteen hours twice in one week.
Do sixteen hours, water only.
Do sixteen hours and get through an ordinary day inside it.
Sit through one wave of hunger without eating, and time how long it lasted.
steps.note: Time it properly. Hunger comes in waves and goes again, usually inside twenty minutes. Knowing that is most of the skill.

steps.test: Do sixteen hours on three separate days in one week.
Do eighteen hours, water only.
Do eighteen hours and take a walk inside it.
Do twenty hours.
Do twenty-four hours — one evening meal to the next evening meal.
steps.note: Water, and salt in it if you feel light-headed. Stop if you feel genuinely unwell; stopping is not failing.

steps.test: Do twenty-four hours on a normal working day, not a quiet one.
Do twenty-eight hours.
Do thirty-two hours, and sleep through part of it.
Do thirty-six hours, and break it properly with a real meal.
steps.note: Break it small and slow — broth, eggs, something cooked. Not a feast. Breaking it badly is the part people get wrong.

categories.name: Creating order
categories.line: Clear it, mend it, give it away, clean the forgotten places. A life flows when the place is in order.

tracks.name: The bedroom
tracks.line: Where the day starts and ends.

steps.test: Clear every surface in the bedroom and put back only what you used this week.
how: The bedside, the top of the drawers, the windowsill, the chair.
Put a thing back only if you used it this week.
Everything else goes in a box by the door.

steps.test: Make the bed properly every morning for a week.
steps.note: Straight cover, pillows plumped, sixty seconds. It is the first thing done each day.

steps.test: Empty the box by the door: bin it, give it, or find each thing a real home.
steps.note: Nothing goes back onto a surface.

steps.test: Clean the bedroom to a close look: under the bed, the skirting, the corners, the light switch.
Wash the bedding, the pillow covers, and the curtains or blind.
Sit in the finished room for ten minutes with nothing in your hands and notice how it feels.
steps.note: This is the test. Order you can feel is the point, not a tidy photo.

tracks.name: The desk
tracks.line: One clear surface to think at.

steps.test: Clear the desk to bare wood, wipe it, and put back the three things you use every day.
Every loose paper into one pile, then through it once: bin, file, or act on it today.
Sort the drawers: one drawer for what you use, everything else out.
Tame the cables: unplug what is not used, coil and label the rest.
Set the desk each evening for the morning: a clear surface and one thing ready to start on. Do it for a week.
Work a whole session at the clear desk and notice the difference.

tracks.name: The wardrobe
tracks.line: Only clothes you are glad to put on.

steps.test: Take every piece of clothing out and put it on the bed. All of it.
Try on anything you are unsure about. Keep only what fits now and what you are glad to wear.
Bag the rest today: give it, sell it, or bin what is worn out.
Put back what stays so you can see every piece at once.
steps.note: Hang or fold by kind. If you cannot see it, you will not wear it.

steps.test: Mend, or take to be mended, anything kept with a button, a hem or a zip gone.
Dress for a week from the finished wardrobe and count how many mornings were quicker.

tracks.name: Broken things
tracks.line: Fix it or let it go.

steps.test: Walk the whole house with a notebook and list every broken thing.
how: Doors, handles, drawers, lamps, chairs.
The dripping tap, the loose shelf, the light that flickers.
Write every one down, however small.

steps.test: Fix three small things from the list today.
steps.note: A screw, a battery, a plug, a hinge. Small counts.

steps.test: For each thing you will not fix, decide today: bin it, or take it to be repaired this week.
Fix one thing that needs a part or a tool: order the part, get the tool, do it.
Fix or remove the last thing on the list.
Keep a page for broken things and clear it every Sunday for a month.

tracks.name: Giving away
tracks.line: What no longer serves you can serve somebody.

steps.test: Fill one bag with things you have not used in a year. Today.
Take it to a charity shop, a friend, or a giving box the same day.
Do the kitchen: gadgets, mugs, tins past their date. One bag out.
Do the books, games and hobby things you have finished with. Pass them on.
Give away one thing that is good and that you like, to somebody who will use it more.
A month on, count what you missed.
steps.note: Almost always nothing. That is the finding.

tracks.name: The phone and the inbox
tracks.line: The clutter you carry in your pocket.

steps.test: Delete every app you have not opened in a month.
Delete the screenshots and the junk photos from the last month. Keep the ones that matter.
how: Open the screenshots album and clear it.
Then the last month of photos: blurred, doubles, receipts already dealt with.
Keep what you would show somebody.

steps.test: Unsubscribe from twenty emails you never read.
steps.note: Search your inbox for the word unsubscribe and work down the list.

steps.test: Get the inbox to empty once: archive, delete, or act.
steps.note: Anything older than a month that nobody is waiting on can be archived without reading it.

steps.test: Clear the home screen to one page of what you use. The rest into folders, or gone.
Turn off every notification that is not a person talking to you.
Keep the inbox at empty by the end of each day for a week.

tracks.name: The forgotten places
tracks.line: Behind, under, on top of, and inside.

steps.test: Clean the windows, inside and out, in one room.
Wash or wipe the blinds and the curtain rail.
Clean behind and under the sink, and the bin itself.
Empty and wipe the fridge, shelf by shelf, and bin what is past.
Wash the curtains, or take them to be cleaned.
The top of the cupboards, the light shades, and the skirting all the way round: one room.
Do one forgotten place every week for a month.

tracks.name: Keeping it
tracks.line: Order that stays.

steps.test: Everything you own has a home: choose one for the five things that never get put away.
Ten minutes every evening putting the day back. Do it for a week.
One in, one out: for a month, nothing new comes in without something going.
A Sunday reset: half an hour that puts the whole place right. Do four of them.
Walk the whole house with a close look. Where has clutter crept back? Deal with it today.
Keep the place in a state you are glad to walk into for three months.
steps.note: Order you can feel, every day, is the finish line. Then it is simply how you live.

tracks.name: Your own things
tracks.line: From four, beside you. Shoes, cover, clothes, books, and one box put right.

steps.test: Put your shoes side by side by the door, the same way round.
Pull the cover up straight on your bed when you get out of it.
Put your clothes in the wash basket at bedtime, without being asked.
steps.note: Without being asked is the hard part. That is the whole step.

steps.test: Put the books back on the shelf the right way up.
Empty one box of toys onto the floor and put every single one back in.
Put away what you were playing with before the next thing comes out, for a whole afternoon.

journey.name: Easy wins
journey.line: Every one of these is a decision rather than a skill. Minutes each, nothing to buy, nothing to learn first. Most people are surprised they had never done them.

journey.name: Courage, worth and asking
journey.line: Deliberately early. Once you can ask for things, walk into anywhere and hear no without flinching, a great many things that looked like they cost money turn out not to. This stage quietly changes what everything after it is worth.
